USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 tariffs in place and use the already-scheduled Trump–Xi G20 meeting to reopen talks, without a new tariff hike and without a rollback. Treat the January 1, 2019 step-up of List 3 from 10% to 25% as leverage to extract a work plan on IP, forced tech transfer, and industrial subsidies—not as an automatic next shot. Do not trade structural demands for another purchases-only truce of the May 19 type; do not add the remaining ~$260B list before Buenos Aires.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high. Combined US coverage is now ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from Sept 24), and China has answered with matching $50B plus 5–10% on ~$60B of US goods. That retaliation is already biting a core US export sector: US goods exports to China fell about 20% from June to November (EXPCH $10.86B to $8.65B), and federal data through mid-October show US soybean sales to China down 94%, with cash prices in the farm belt below $7/bu versus nearly $10 a year earlier and USDA aid covering less than half of estimated losses. The original 301 problem is also still live: the March 22 USTR findings on IP and tech transfer have not been remedied, and late-October comments from Kudlow and others were that Beijing had still not answered on those structural items. That combination sits well below the +0.5 US anchor (national GDP drag is not yet material). US industrial production is still rising, Michigan sentiment remains high at 97.5, and CPI is contained; Moody's public estimate of a ~0.2pp US growth hit is modest next to China's 0.3–0.5pp. The US still has leverage—CNY has weakened ~9% toward 6.92, China IP growth has cooled, and Xi agreed on Nov 1 to a G20 meeting—but October VIX spikes above 25, a stronger dollar, and rising Fed funds (2.20%) mean the US economy has less spare room to absorb a further shock. Action should therefore stay near hold/negotiate. Escalating now (List 3 to 25% early, or the remaining ~$260B list floated in late October) would hit consumer goods and supply chains, deepen farm-belt losses before Brazil's spring harvest, and poison the only live leader-level channel. Rolling back or locking in purchase commitments would repeat May 19–29, when a purchases joint statement was walked back within ten days and produced no structural movement. Midterms (Democrats taking the House, GOP Senate) do not constrain unilateral tariff authority and are bipartisan-hawkish on China, so there is no domestic need to concede—and no excuse to skip the G20 window.
key_factors: Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese imports, with List 3 scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
China retaliation has crushed a key US export sector: EXPCH -20% since June; soybean sales to China -94% through mid-October
Core 301 grievances (IP, forced tech transfer, industrial policy) remain unaddressed; May purchases truce collapsed in 10 days
US macro still solid (IP up, sentiment ~97.5) but October vol, Fed tightening, and a stronger dollar reduce room to escalate
Nov 1 Trump–Xi call set a G20 meeting; talks otherwise on hiatus—best use of leverage is negotiate without new commitments
Midterms flip the House but do not change unilateral tariff power or the bipartisan hawkish consensus on China

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, WTO case, and investment restrictions.
US-China joint statement: China agrees to significantly increase purchases; Mnuchin says trade war is on hold.
White House announces US will proceed with Section 301 25% tariffs on ~$50B; truce collapses.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% on ~$200B effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
List 3 takes effect at 10%; China retaliates 5–10% on ~$60B; combined US Section 301 coverage ~$250B.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
US exports to China fell from $10.86B (June) to $8.65B (November), about -20% over the window.
Michigan consumer sentiment still high at 97.5 (November), only a modest decline over the lookback.
VIX spiked to 25.23 on Oct 24 and was still 16.36 on Nov 7, up ~27% over the window.
CNY weakened from 6.34 in mid-May to 6.92 on Nov 7 (~9%), offsetting some US tariff pressure.
American soybean sales to China down 94% from last year's harvest through mid-October; local elevator bids below $7/bu vs nearly $10 last year; $3.6B aid covers less than half of North Dakota losses.
Trump-Xi call cheered markets but advisers said nothing much had changed; talks on hiatus until G20; soybean farmers hurt while steel mills benefit.
Moody's: latest tariffs could cut US growth ~0.2pp and China 0.3–0.5pp next year; List 3 to rise to 25% Jan 1.
Report Trump could tariff an additional $260B as soon as December; List 3 10% scheduled to 25% in January unless a deal is struck.
Democrats take the House, GOP keeps Senate; both parties support a tougher China stance; Oval Office retains unilateral tariff power.
Kudlow (Oct 23): China has yet to agree to US asks on tech transfer and IP theft; leaders will meet 'for a bit' at G20.
